items.title: Classical commentary
items.context: Commentary organizes classics, inherited interpretation, textual criticism and teaching into transmissible knowledge structures.

items.title: Form and emptiness
items.context: Form and emptiness is one of the Heart Sutra's most cited expressions, but it must be read within a specific version, passage structure and Prajnaparamita context.

items.title: Naturalness and self-so
items.context: In early Daoist texts, ziran first concerns being so of itself and should not be equated directly with the modern category of nature.

items.title: Pilgrimage and transmission
items.context: Pilgrimage became durable knowledge transmission through translation, cataloguing, teaching and institutional collaboration.

items.title: Ritual and order
items.context: Li can refer to texts and norms as well as concrete ritual, relational identity and order within state education.

items.title: Translation as institution
items.context: Translation is not only the exchange of words; it depends on sites, people, versions, review and relations of power.

items.title: An Lushan Rebellion begins
items.context: War beginning in 755 disrupted the two capitals and changed the demographic, fiscal and institutional environment of religious life.

items.title: End of the An Lushan Rebellion
items.context: The end of warfare around 763 did not restore the pre-war order but opened a long restructuring of finance, regional power and institutions.

items.title: The Buddha's first sermon at Sarnath
items.context: Early Buddhist texts and later heritage traditions remember Sarnath as the place where the Buddha taught his first disciples.

items.title: Confucius visits Zhou to ask Laozi about rites
items.context: The Shiji preserves Confucius's visit to Laozi in Zhou as an early historiographical entry into a Dao–Ru encounter.

items.title: Establishment of the Great Ci'en Monastery
items.context: The monastery created a new institutional setting for Buddhism, translation and imperial patronage in Chang'an.

items.title: Compilation project of the Corrected Meanings of the Five Classics
items.context: A multi-year early Tang editorial project brought commentarial traditions into state education and examination knowledge.

items.title: First construction of the Great Wild Goose Pagoda
items.context: The initial phase around 652 linked the preservation of texts and images with translation and visible urban architecture.

items.title: Huichang religious policies
items.context: Policies around 845 sharply changed the property, personnel and public standing of Buddhist and other religious institutions.

items.title: Institutional expansion in the Kaiyuan era
items.context: The Kaiyuan era provides a range for studying expansion in court, education, religious institutions and transregional exchange.

items.title: The founding and unification of the Sui
items.context: The founding and unification of the Sui provides political context for Sui–Tang institutions, capitals and networks of knowledge.

items.title: Foundation of the Tang dynasty
items.context: The dynastic transition of 618 reorganized the political, educational and religious resource environment of Chang'an.

items.title: The Tang-end political transition
items.context: The political transition around 907 marks the exhibition's Sui–Tang boundary while reminding us that institutions and textual networks do not disappear in one year.

items.title: Establishment of the Wu Zhou
items.context: The political transition of 690 changed imperial representation, the two-capital system and the allocation of religious resources.

items.title: Xuanzang departs Chang'an
items.context: Around 629, Xuanzang's journey connected Chang'an with pilgrimage networks across the Hexi Corridor, Central Asia and South Asia.

items.title: Xuanzang returns to Chang'an
items.context: After Xuanzang returned to Chang'an, pilgrimage experience became long-term work in translation, teaching and monastic institutions.

items.title: Yijing departs by sea
items.context: Around 671, Yijing travelled south by sea, showing that pilgrimage and transmission were not limited to an overland route west of Chang'an.

items.title: Yijing returns to Tang territory
items.context: Around 695, Yijing's return brought maritime travel experience into translation, writing and institutional networks.

items.title: Cheng Xuanying
items.context: Cheng Xuanying offers an entry into early Tang interpretation of the Daodejing and Zhuangzi and its Daoist knowledge networks.

items.title: Confucius (Kong Qiu)
items.context: Confucius is a recognisable gateway into Confucian classics, education and political ethics; sayings in the Analects must be separated from disciple records, compilation layers and later classical reception.

items.title: Jizang
items.context: Jizang's teaching and commentary provide a case for Buddhist thought, textual interpretation and urban networks across the Sui–Tang transition.

items.title: Kong Yingda
items.context: Kong Yingda represents how Tang classical learning entered state education, commentary and institutional knowledge production.

items.title: Laozi (Li Er)
items.context: Laozi is a recognisable gateway into Daoist classicism, but the Li Er biography, the sage-name Laozi, the formation of the Daodejing and the later Taishang Laojun image must remain distinct layers.

items.title: Li Shimin
items.context: Li Shimin's courtly, educational and religious institutional context helps explain why Chang'an became a meeting point for different networks of knowledge and belief.

items.title: Śākyamuni Buddha (Gautama)
items.context: Śākyamuni is a central gateway into Buddhist thought and pilgrimage geography, but fragmentary early-text biographies, later Buddha legends and sacred narratives must remain layered.

items.title: Sima Chengzhen
items.context: Sima Chengzhen connects mountain cultivation, Daoist lineages and Tang imperial patronage.

items.title: Wu Zhao (Wu Zetian)
items.context: Wu Zhao's political practice and religious patronage make the institutions, rituals and later memories of Chang'an and Luoyang available for comparison.

items.title: Xuanzang
items.context: Xuanzang connects a pilgrimage for learning with translation and institutional life in Chang'an.

items.title: Yan Shigu
items.context: Yan Shigu connects early Tang textual editing and commentary with state knowledge projects.

items.title: Yijing
items.context: Yijing connects maritime pilgrimage, learning in South Asia and the production of Chinese Buddhist translations.

items.title: Chang'an Daoist monastic network
items.context: Daoist activity in Chang'an relied on multiple institutions, ritual services, ordination records and court connections rather than one building.

items.title: Chang'an translation-bureau network
items.context: Translation was collaborative work supported by monastic space, language roles, textual checking and imperial patronage.

items.title: Great Ci'en Monastery
items.context: Great Ci'en Monastery is a core institutional entry for connecting Xuanzang, translation, monastic networks and Chang'an's urban space.

items.title: Guozijian
items.context: The Guozijian connects the Five Classics, commentary, examination and state education within a traceable institutional line.

items.title: Hongwen Institute
items.context: The Hongwen Institute offers an institutional entry into Tang court collections, scholarly consultation and education.

items.title: Louguan Daoist institution
items.context: As an institutional record, Louguan helps separate Laozi legend, Daoist figures, monastic space and later sacred-site narratives.

items.title: Classical commentary manuscript record (object placeholder)
items.context: The object card connects the Corrected Meanings and Guozijian to manuscripts, folios and practices of reading.

items.title: Daodejing commentary manuscript record (object placeholder)
items.context: The object record reserves an archive entry for manuscript form, writing layers and provenance of Tang Daodejing commentaries.

items.title: Daoist institutional inscription rubbing (object placeholder)
items.context: Inscriptions and rubbings can anchor institutions, figures, dates and patronage in verifiable textual objects.

items.title: Official-learning ritual object record (object placeholder)
items.context: A ritual object can connect the concept of li with school space, participants and concrete action.

items.title: Heart Sutra manuscript leaf (object placeholder)
items.context: The object card places a Heart Sutra passage within paper, ink, writing, preservation and circulation, but is not yet tied to a specific collection.

items.title: State-school classics scroll (object placeholder)
items.context: A scroll object can show how classics entered official learning through copying, collation and teaching.

items.title: Longmen dedicatory inscription record (object placeholder)
items.context: A dedicatory inscription can connect image, donor, vow, date and cave location as a traceable object.

items.title: Inscription record for a translation institution (object placeholder)
items.context: The object card separates translation institutions from biography and looks for material carriers in buildings, inscriptions and institutional memory.

items.title: Translation catalogue manuscript (object placeholder)
items.context: Catalogue objects can record translated titles, versions, attribution and institutional organization of textual circulation.

items.title: A Dao that can be spoken
items.context: The opening of the Daodejing frames a problem among language, naming and constancy.

items.title: Do not impose on others what you do not desire
items.context: The answer expresses shu as restraint in treating others, beginning from what one would not wish to bear oneself.

items.title: Form is not different from emptiness
items.context: This line circulated widely in Chinese Buddhism, but it must be read within its paragraph and textual version.

items.title: Highest goodness is like water
items.context: The water metaphor connects benefiting things, non-contention and dwelling in low places as relational qualities.

items.title: Humans follow earth; earth follows heaven
items.context: The line arranges humans, earth, heaven, the Dao and naturalness in a layered order that must be read in its received-text context.

items.title: To learn and practise at due times
items.context: The Analects opens by connecting learning, repeated practice and pleasure.

items.title: In learning one increases; in the Dao one decreases
items.context: The passage contrasts accumulation in learning with a practice of decreasing toward non-forcing.

items.title: These dharmas have the characteristic of emptiness
items.context: The line places emptiness within a description of dharmas and helps demonstrate the relation among concept, passage and version layers.

items.title: Seeing the five aggregates as empty
items.context: The line compresses seeing, the five aggregates and emptiness into a short phrase that must be read in a specific version and context.

items.title: No wisdom and no attainment
items.context: The line invites a distinction between the sutra's context of non-attainment and a modern denial of knowledge.

items.title: Conquer the self and return to ritual
items.context: The line connects humaneness with self-restraint and ritual practice, and was repeatedly reinterpreted in political and educational settings.

items.title: When three walk together, there is surely a teacher for me
items.context: The saying places learning in companionship, discernment of strengths and self-correction.

items.title: This is the noble truth of suffering
items.context: The short line keeps Buddhist teaching within the textual setting of the first turning at Sarnath rather than turning it into a context-free modern maxim.

items.title: This is the noble truth of stress
items.context: This passage shares the SN 56.11 locator with the Pāli excerpt while preserving Thanissaro's English rendering of dukkha.

items.title: Chang'an
items.context: Chang'an compressed court, state education, monasteries, Daoist institutions, markets and international travellers into one city.

items.title: Dunhuang
items.context: Dunhuang connects Buddhist art, textual preservation, travel routes and multilingual culture.

items.title: Great Wild Goose Pagoda site
items.context: The site connects Xuanzang, translation, textual preservation and the urban space of Chang'an.

items.title: Longmen Grottoes
items.context: Longmen brings Luoyang, imperial patronage, Buddhist images and inscriptions into one material landscape.

items.title: Luoyang
items.context: Luoyang connects imperial politics, transport networks, Buddhist transmission and classical culture as a counterpoint to Chang'an.

items.title: Mount Wutai
items.context: Mount Wutai combines a real mountain landscape, monastic networks and Buddhist sacred narratives, making the museum's two-layer geography visible.

items.title: Nalanda
items.context: Nalanda places the pilgrimages of Xuanzang and Yijing within a concrete institution and transregional network rather than an abstract India.

items.title: Kucha
items.context: Kucha keeps a pilgrimage route from becoming a straight line from Chang'an to India; it was a region where languages, religions and media intersected.

items.title: Sarnath
items.context: Sarnath connects Śākyamuni, the first-turning-of-the-Dharma tradition, early monastic memory and later Buddhist pilgrimage to a real archaeological place.

items.title: Zhongnan Mountains
items.context: The Zhongnan Mountains are a real landscape near Chang'an and a layered setting for cultivation, reclusion and religious narrative.

items.title: Chang'an–Luoyang imperial corridor
items.context: The route organizes political, educational, religious and human movement between the two capitals as a spatial research frame.

items.title: Xuanzang's western pilgrimage route
items.context: The route places Chang'an, the Hexi Corridor, Central Asia and South Asia in one research view without treating every node as a verified day-by-day itinerary.

items.title: Received text of the Analects
items.context: An Alpha version record for the received chapters of the Analects.

items.title: Received text of the Daodejing
items.context: An Alpha version record for the received chapters of the Daodejing.

items.title: Sui–Tang Daoist institutional research collection
items.context: This version is a catalogue placeholder that reminds the editorial team to replace the collection with citable texts or records.

items.title: Pāli digital version of the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta
items.context: The version layer records the Pāli text's reference, language and digital-edition context.

items.title: Thanissaro English translation of SN 56.11
items.context: This version keeps an English translation witness separate from the Pāli version so translator choices can be compared without treating translation as the source text.

items.title: Received edited version of the Corrected Meanings
items.context: The version layer separates the specific edited text, fascicles and citation locator from the general text record.

items.title: Received edited version of the Record of the Western Regions
items.context: This version record supports passage locators, translation and variant comparison for the Record of the Western Regions.

items.title: Received Chinese version of the Heart Sutra
items.context: A version placeholder for the first passage display; the precise edition remains under review.

items.title: Analects
items.context: The Analects preserves early Confucian discussions of ethics, education and politics through sayings and encounters associated with Confucius and his disciples.

items.title: Daodejing
items.context: The formation, compilation and attribution of the Daodejing have several historical layers, and later Daoist and philosophical traditions repeatedly reinterpreted it.

items.title: Sui–Tang Daoist institutional records
items.context: This research-layer text collection helps distinguish Daoist biographies, institutional history and later genealogical narratives.

items.title: Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta
items.context: The Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta preserves a transmitted discourse tradition in which the Buddha teaches the five mendicants at Sarnath.

items.title: Corrected Meanings of the Five Classics
items.context: The Corrected Meanings provides an entry into how Tang classical commentary entered state education and regimes of interpretation.

items.title: Record of the Western Regions of the Great Tang
items.context: The Record turns a pilgrim's travel experience into an account of geography, institutions, cities and religious sites.

items.title: Heart Sutra
items.context: The Heart Sutra presents Prajñāpāramitā thought in a highly condensed form and became one of the most widely circulated texts in Chinese Buddhism.
